newsitem.title: HUNGARY: ROMANIA, HUNGARY SET UP JOINT PEACEKEEPING UNIT.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA, HUNGARY SET UP JOINT PEACEKEEPING UNIT.

text.p: The defence ministers of Hungary and Romania confirmed a warming of relations between the two countries on Monday by setting up a joint military unit and signing an accord on the protection of military secrets.

"We have signed an agreement on the protection of secrets that will enable...close military cooperation," Hungarian Defence Minister Gyorgy Keleti told reporters after signing the accord with his Romanian counterpart Victor Babiuc in the Hungarian city of Debrecen near the Romanian border.
"We have also agreed to set up a joint Hungarian-Romanian peacekeeping battalion for use with NATO, the United Nations and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe."

Hungary's state secretary at the defence ministry responsible for NATO integration, Istvan Gyarmati, told Reuters after the meeting that he and his Romanian counterpart had been entrusted with the task of working out the details of the new unit.
"The new agreement on the protection of military confidential information will facilitate the creation of a joint peacekeeping battalion which the ministers also decided (to set up)."
"We will meet next month with the General Staffs to work out the details," he said.
Gyarmati added that the Romanian part of the new battalion will be based in Romania and the Hungarian part in Hungary with a joint command and joint exercises.

Analysts believe the agreements reached on Monday will enhance both countries chances of early NATO membership and could mean Romania joining current favourites the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary in the first group of new members to NATO to be announced at the aliiance's next summit in July.
Keleti told Reuters earlier the agreement on the protection and exchange of military secrets was Hungary's first with an East European neighbour.
"It will entitle us to exchange important miltary information," he said. "So far we only have such agreements with the United States, Germany and Sweden."

Bucharest's new centre-right government, elected last November after seven years of rule by ex-communists, is seeking to boost Romania's chances of early admission to NATO by developing a new partnership with Hungary.

New president Emil Constantinescu appointed two leaders of Hungary's ethnic minority to his government while Foreign Mnister Adrian Severin's first trip abroad was to Hungary to exchange ratified basic treaty documents with his Hungarian counterpart, Laszlo Kovacs.

The treaty, signed in September, aims to end old quarrels by guaranteeing Romania's western borders and ensuring the rights of Romania's 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians and is seen as vital to the ambitions of Romania and Hungary to move closer to Europe and NATO. REUTER
